taxonomy.note: Current Kew/POWO accepts Nassella leucotricha; older Texas literature commonly uses Stipa leucotricha.

evidence: Hays — UT Plant Resources Center Flora of Purola Preserve, N. Hays County explicitly records Nassella leucotricha.

Travis — Travis County environmental documentation explicitly records Texas wintergrass (Nassella leucotricha) in native grassland/woodland vegetation; Barton Creek Habitat Preserve research also lists it as a dominant herbaceous species in Travis County.
Williamson — UT Plant Resources Center Vascular Plants of Williamson County provides a detailed treatment under the synonym Stipa leucotricha.
target_zone_range.guardrail: No county occurrence inferred from statewide or ecoregion distribution alone.

morphology.look_here_first: Look for a cool-season, wispy bunchgrass with a loose panicle and single extremely long twisted awns. Each fertile floret carries one awn—not the three-awned fork of Aristida.
diagnostic_traits: perennial cool-season bunchgrass, green and actively growing through cool months when many warm-season prairie grasses are dormant
culms commonly 35–70 cm, fertile shoots sometimes longer
dark-green narrow blades with short stiff/bristly hairs and rough surfaces
loose open panicle with long slender lower branches
single-flowered spikelets with one very long twisted/bent awn, often 6–10 cm
lemma/seed has a sharp callus or barb-like base that gives the speargrass impression
after seed shed, persistent pale/white glumes can give the panicle an oat-like look

confusers.separator: Threeawns split into three awn branches from each fertile lemma; Texas wintergrass has one long twisted awn per floret.
Little bluestem is a warm-season bunchgrass with branched upper culms and short fuzzy racemes; Texas wintergrass is cool-season with a loose open panicle and conspicuous single long awns.

diagnostic_roles: hairy narrow leaf blade and ligule/collar
